Case Vignette: "Samira"

Samira is a 68-year-old married woman of Middle Eastern descent who has worked as a prison guard for the past 22 years. She presents for therapy at the urging of her husband, who has grown concerned about her withdrawal, irritability, and difficulty sleeping over the past six months. Samira agrees that something has changed, though she struggles to name it. She is a sturdy, composed woman with a direct gaze, but her hands tremble slightly as she settles into the chair.

The traumatic event occurred eight months ago, on a late evening shift in the medium-security unit where Samira works. She was conducting a routine cell check when an inmate, a man in his early thirties with a history of violence, ambushed her from behind. He had fashioned a shank from a melted toothbrush and pressed it against her throat before she could react. He demanded she open the cell door for another inmate, but she refused. In the struggle that followed, he struck her twice in the face with his fist, breaking her nose and fracturing her orbital bone. She managed to press her panic button, and other guards subdued him within minutes. Samira spent three days in the hospital and underwent surgery to repair the bone around her eye.

In the weeks immediately following the assault, Samira returned to work after a month of medical leave. She told herself she had to get back on the horse, that she had survived worse in her life—she had fled her home country as a young woman, had raised three children while working double shifts. She minimized the event, even to her husband. But within two months, she began to notice changes she could not ignore. She now avoids the block where the assault occurred, requesting reassignment to the administrative wing, a move that feels shameful to her. She finds herself scanning every inmate’s hands for weapons, her heart racing when she hears footsteps behind her in the corridor. She startles violently at the sound of a metal door slamming, sometimes dropping her keys.

At home, Samira has become hypervigilant in ways that baffle her. She insists on checking the locks on every door three times before bed. She has stopped watching the evening news because images of violence—even fictional ones—make her feel as though she is back in that cell, the cold metal of the shank against her throat. She has recurrent nightmares, though she cannot recall their details upon waking, only a sense of dread that lingers throughout the morning. She has stopped cooking her favorite meals, a hobby she once loved, because standing at the stove with her back to the kitchen door makes her feel trapped.

Her marriage has grown strained. Her husband, a gentle retired teacher, tries to comfort her, but she snaps at him when he touches her unexpectedly. She feels disconnected from him, as though a pane of glass has been placed between her and everyone she loves. She has not told her adult children about the assault, fearing they will worry or, worse, view her as weak. She has always been the strong one, the matriarch, the woman who survived war and displacement through sheer will. This new fragility feels like a betrayal of her own identity.

Samira’s PCL-5 score is 35, indicating a moderate level of PTSD symptoms. She describes her mood as “flat” and admits she no longer looks forward to weekends, which she once spent gardening or visiting her grandchildren. She feels a constant, low-level guilt: she believes she should have seen the attack coming, should have been more alert. She replays the moment in her mind, wondering if she could have done something differently. She does not cry when she tells me this; her face remains still, a practiced composure that has served her for decades.

She has come to therapy because she is tired of feeling afraid in her own skin. She wants to return to the person she was before, though she is not sure that person exists anymore.
